what: Murphy Oil is an independent oil and gas producer. Its main fields are in the US Gulf of Mexico, Canada (Tupper Montney gas and Kaybob Duvernay) and the Eagle Ford shale in Texas, and it explores offshore in places such as Vietnam and Côte d’Ivoire.
customers: Refiners and traders who buy its crude oil, and gas utilities and marketers who buy its natural gas.
money: Crude oil and natural gas liquids, mostly from the Gulf of Mexico and the Eagle Ford.
Mostly Canadian gas from the Montney.
moat: Experience operating deep-water fields in the Gulf of Mexico, a niche with high costs to enter, and a low-cost Canadian gas position. As a mid-sized producer it has no pricing power; it takes the oil price.
risks: Profit follows the oil price: net income fell from $965M in 2022 to $104M in 2025 as prices eased.
Exploration is risky; a dry well offshore can cost hundreds of millions.
Offshore production is exposed to hurricanes in the Gulf of Mexico.
Production in some fields is declining and needs new investment to replace it.
opportunities: Cash from operations of $1.77B over the last twelve months is large relative to a $4.6B market value.
Debt of $2.3B against $5.4B of equity is moderate.
Shares outstanding fell from 157M in 2022 to 144M in 2025 through buybacks.
A discovery in Vietnam or West Africa could add a new growth area.
watch: Oil prices and production volumes, and the results of its exploration wells.
view: Murphy is a straightforward oil producer valued like one in a weak market: about 10 times trailing earnings, 7.4 times forward, and an enterprise value of roughly 3.5 times EBITDA. Earnings have fallen every year since 2022 because oil prices have fallen, not because the business has deteriorated. Cash from operations of $1.77 billion over the last twelve months is still large against a $4.6 billion market value.

One caution on our own data: the capital spending figure on this page is too low for a company that drills deep-water wells, so the free cash flow shown is overstated. Murphy spends roughly a billion dollars a year to keep production flat, and a sensible estimate of free cash flow is a fraction of operating cash flow, not nearly all of it.

The investment is a bet on the oil price plus an exploration option. Murphy has been cutting its share count and keeps debt moderate, so if oil holds up, shareholders benefit. If it falls further, earnings and the dividend come under pressure. I would call it fairly priced for a mid-sized producer: not a bargain, not expensive, and only as good as your view on oil.
bull: Oil prices recover, a new discovery adds growth and buybacks keep shrinking the share count.
bear: Oil stays weak, exploration disappoints and the costs of keeping production flat eat most of the cash.
